summary: This document extends the basic IP fast reroute mechanism in RFC 5286 to give extra backup connectivity for point-to-point link failures when the basic mechanisms cannot offer any.

plainLanguage.summary: When a link fails, a router needs another neighbour that can still reach the destination. In a ring there often is none. This document builds a tunnel to a remote router that can, and uses that router as the backup path. It measured the result in 14 real service provider networks.

questions: ip fast reroute remote loop-free alternate
how does ip fast reroute work
subtitle: How to keep traffic flowing when a link fails and no local backup path exists.

tldr.problem: A router that loses a link can usually send the traffic elsewhere, but only to a neighbour that can still reach the destination without the broken link. Ring topologies often have no such neighbour, so those links end up unprotected.
tldr.mechanism: The router that detects the failure pre-builds a tunnel to a remote PQ node, a router that is reachable without the failed link and can reach the destination. The tunnel endpoint is found by intersecting the extended P-space of the repairing router with the Q-space of the far end.
tldr.outcome: In the RFC's study of 14 real service provider topologies, remote LFA gave close to 100% protection against link failure in 11 of them. It covers point-to-point link failures only; node failures are out of scope.

facts.label: Highest number of targeted LDP sessions

today: RFC 7490 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2015. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the standard way to add backup connectivity for point-to-point link failures where plain loop-free alternates cannot help.

sections.title: Why LFAs Leave Some Links Unprotected
sections.content:
IP Fast Reroute (IPFRR) is a framework for keeping traffic flowing when a link fails, and RFC 5286 describes a basic mechanism using Loop-Free Alternates (LFAs). A router detects the failure and sends the affected traffic to a neighbour that can still reach the destination without going back over the failed link. That mechanism gives good repair coverage in many topologies, especially highly meshed ones.

Some topologies, notably rings, are not well protected by LFAs alone. The reason is that no neighbour of the Point of Local Repair (PLR) has a cost to the destination that avoids the failure and is cheaper than the cost through the failure.

This document extends the LFA approach to cover many of those cases by tunnelling the packets that need repair to a node that is both reachable from the PLR and able to reach the destination. The technique is directed at link failures. It covers the case where the repair first hop is reached over a broadcast or non-broadcast multi-access (NBMA) link such as a LAN, and the case where the P or Q node is attached over such a link, but not the more complicated case where the failed interface itself is a broadcast or NBMA link. The repair path is assumed to be confined to a single area or to the level two routing domain; in all other cases the chosen PQ node should be regarded as a tunnel adjacency and the considerations in Section 6 of RFC 5286 should be taken into account.
sections.plainLanguage: Fast reroute means a router sends traffic around a failed link instead of dropping it. It works when a neighbour can reach the destination without the broken link. Rings often have no such neighbour, and this document covers those cases.

sections.title: P-space, Q-space and the PQ Node
sections.content:
The document uses the terms defined in RFC 5714 and adds a few of its own.

  • A repair tunnel is a tunnel established for the purpose of providing a virtual neighbour that is a Loop-Free Alternate.
  • The P-space of a router with respect to a protected link is the set of routers reachable from that router using the pre-convergence shortest paths without any of those paths, including equal-cost path splits, transiting that protected link.
  • The extended P-space of the protecting router is the union of the P-spaces of its neighbours, with the neighbour reached over the protected link excluded.
  • The Q-space of a router with respect to a protected link is the set of routers from which that router can be reached without any path, including equal-cost path splits, transiting the protected link.
  • A PQ node of a node S with respect to a protected link S-E is a node that is in both the P-space, or the extended P-space, of S and in the Q-space of E. The repair tunnel endpoint is chosen from the set of PQ nodes.

Remote LFA (RLFA) is the use of a PQ node rather than a neighbour of the repairing node as the next hop in an LFA repair. In the document's notation X-Y means the path from X to Y over the link directly connecting them, while X->Y refers to the shortest path from X to Y.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names four sets of routers. The P-space is what a router can reach without the failed link. The extended P-space adds what its neighbours can reach. The Q-space is what can reach the far end without the failed link. A PQ node is in both the extended P-space and the Q-space.

sections.title: Repairing a Ring with a Tunnel
sections.content:
The problem appears in a simple ring. S and E are joined by one link and the rest of the ring runs S, A, B, C, D, E. If all link costs are equal, traffic transiting link S-E cannot be fully protected by LFAs. The destination C is an Equal-Cost Multipath from S, so traffic to C can be protected when S-E fails, but traffic to D and E cannot.

The document describes extensions to the basic repair mechanism in which tunnels provide additional logical links that can then be used as loop-free alternates where none exist in the original topology. In the ring, S can reach A, B and C without going via S-E, and these form S's extended P-space with respect to S-E. The routers that can reach E without going through S-E are D and C, which form E's Q-space. B is not in E's Q-space, because B has equal-cost paths to E and the forwarder at S might send a packet to E via S-E. The single node in both sets is C, so C is selected as the repair tunnel's endpoint. With a tunnel between S and C, C becomes a direct neighbour of S and an LFA for D and E.

The tunnel is only used for repair traffic and MUST NOT be used for normal traffic, so the non-failure traffic distribution is not disrupted. Operations, Administration and Maintenance traffic used to verify the viability of the repair MAY traverse the tunnel before a failure. The technique is not restricted to rings; it is a general mechanism that can enhance the protection LFAs provide. It suits incremental deployment, including in a network that is already deploying LFA, and the computation of the repair path takes place exclusively on the repairing node.
sections.plainLanguage: In a ring, one router sits next to the broken link and has no backup neighbour. This document builds a tunnel to a router on the far side of the ring and treats that router as a new neighbour. Traffic then goes round the ring and reaches its destination.

sections.title: Repair Paths and Repair Tunnels
sections.content:
As with LFA FRR, when a router detects an adjacent link failure it uses one or more repair paths in place of the failed link. Repair paths are precomputed in anticipation of later failures so they can be activated promptly when a failure is detected.

A tunneled repair path tunnels traffic to a staging point in the network from which, in the absence of a worse-than-anticipated failure, the traffic will travel to its destination using normal forwarding without looping back. This is equivalent to providing a virtual loop-free alternate to supplement the physical ones, hence the name remote LFA FRR. In its simplest form, when a link cannot be entirely protected with local LFA neighbours, the protecting router seeks the help of a remote LFA staging point.

The tunnel must not traverse the protected link. It terminates at some intermediate router between S and E, not at E itself: if it were possible to construct a tunnel from S to E, a conventional LFA would have been sufficient.

The repair tunnel endpoint must be reachable from the tunnel source without traversing the failed link, and when released from the tunnel, packets must proceed towards their destination without being attracted back over the failed link. Provided both requirements are met, packets forwarded over the repair tunnel reach their destination and do not loop after a single link failure. In some topologies no endpoint will satisfy both properties. For example, if the ring had a cost of four for link B-C while the remaining links cost one, a tunnel from S to C could not be established without resorting to some form of source routing.

Several tunnel mechanisms can supply the repair path, such as IP-in-IP and Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE). In an MPLS-enabled network using LDP, a simple label stack can be used instead: the outer label is the neighbour's label for the repair tunnel endpoint and the inner label is the endpoint's label for the packet destination, which requires a targeted LDP session to the endpoint. The choice of mechanism is outside the scope of the document. The repair tunnel used MUST be provisioned beforehand in anticipation of the failure, and since the location of the repair tunnels is dynamically determined, they must be established automatically. Multiple repair tunnels may share a tunnel endpoint.

Not all links need a tunneled repair path. If E can already be protected by an LFA, then S-E needs no repair tunnel, because every destination normally reachable through E must also be protectable by an LFA. Tunneled repair paths, which may be calculated per prefix, are only required for links that have neither a link nor a per-prefix LFA.

Protecting against worse failures is out of scope: node failures, the failure of a Shared Risk Link Group, independent concurrent failures of multiple links, and broadcast or NBMA links. When the failure is a node failure rather than a point-to-point link failure, there is a danger that the RLFA repair will loop, because two or more of E's neighbours, each with E as the next hop to some destination, may repair via the other neighbour and then E. The document lists three ways to reduce that risk: drop a packet that arrives on the interface also used to reach the first hop of the RLFA path; require that the path from the remote LFA repair target to the destination never passes through E; or require that where a packet may pass through another neighbour of E, that node is downstream, that is, strictly closer to the destination than the repairing node. The first accepts that loops may form and suppresses them by dropping packets, which may also drop legitimate packets. The other two prevent the formation of a loop but reduce repair coverage and add complexity. An operator is advised to analyse the consequences and probability of node failure in their own network.
sections.plainLanguage: The backup path is a tunnel built before the failure happens, so traffic can be pushed into it the moment the link goes down. The tunnel must avoid the failed link, and the router at the far end of it must not send the traffic back over the failed link. Several kinds of tunnel can be used; the document leaves that choice to the operator.

sections.title: Computing the Tunnel Endpoint
sections.content:
Computing the repair path for link S-E means finding the set of routers reachable from S without traversing S-E and matching it with the set of routers from which E can be reached by normal forwarding without traversing S-E.

  • The P-space is the set of routers that can be reached from S on the shortest path tree without traversing S-E. It is obtained by computing a shortest path tree rooted at S and excising the subtree reached via link S-E, including routers that are members of an equal-cost multipath set that includes S-E. In cost terms, a router P is in the P-space when the shortest path cost from S to P is strictly less than the cost from S to E to P.
  • The extended P-space is the union of the P-spaces of S's neighbours, calculated by computing a shortest path tree at each neighbour except E and excising the subtree reached via N to S to E. A router P is in it when the cost from N to P is strictly less than the cost from N to S to E to P. The extended P-space allows greater repair coverage and is the preferred approach, because the initial hop of the repair path need not be subject to S's normal forwarding decision.
  • The Q-space is the set of routers from which E can be reached by normal forwarding without traversing S-E. It is obtained by computing a reverse shortest path tree rooted at E and excising the subtree that might traverse the protected link. A router Q is in it when the cost from Q to E is strictly less than the cost from Q to S to E.

The nodes in both the extended P-space and the Q-space are the viable repair tunnel endpoints, the PQ nodes. The Q-space of E is used as a proxy for the Q-space of each destination, since computing it per destination would in the worst case require an SPF computation per destination, which is not considered scalable.

Several endpoints will often be available, and all of them deliver the packets correctly. The document RECOMMENDS the member of the set with the lowest cost from S, because choosing the closest maximizes the opportunity for the traffic to be load balanced once it is released from the tunnel. In the event of a tie, the router with the lowest node identifier SHOULD be selected. Selecting a PQ node that is downstream of the destination with respect to the repairing node prevents loops when the failure is worse than expected, but reduces the repair coverage, so operators are advised to determine whether adequate coverage is achieved before enabling that feature.

The document then gives a cost-based algorithm in pseudocode. It computes a forward SPF from the repairing node, an SPF at each neighbour to extend the P-space, a reverse SPF to compute the Q-space, intersects the two sets, and applies the downstream constraint if the implementation wants to guarantee no looping on a worse-than-protected failure. The algorithm covers the case where the repair first hop or the P or Q node is attached over a broadcast or NBMA link, but not the case where the failed interface is such a link.
sections.plainLanguage: To find the remote router, the router works out two sets: the routers it can reach without the failed link, and the routers that can reach the far end without the failed link. A router in both sets can be used. The document recommends the one with the lowest cost from the repairing router.

sections.title: A Service Provider Topology
sections.content:
The document works through a topology that is commonly deployed and is not fully protected by LFAs alone. Two provider edge routers, PE1 and PE2, are connected in the same site, and two core routers, P1 and P2, may be geographically separated. To guarantee the lowest latency path to and from all other remote provider edge routers, the shortest path normally follows the geographical distance of the site locations, so a lower IGP metric of 5 is assigned between PE1 and PE2. A high metric of 1000 is set on the P-PE links to prevent the provider edge routers carrying transit traffic, and the provider edge routers are not individually dual-homed in order to reduce costs. This is a common topology in service provider networks.

When the link between PE1 and P1 fails, PE1 does not have an LFA for traffic reachable via P1. By symmetry, if the link between PE2 and P2 fails, PE2 does not have an LFA for traffic reachable via P2. Increasing the metric between PE1 and PE2 to allow the LFA would affect normal traffic performance by potentially increasing the latency.

Full protection can be provided with the technique described in the document: PE1 chooses P2 as the remote LFA repair target node, and PE2 chooses P1 as its remote LFA repair target.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example is a network where two provider edge routers sit together and two core routers sit apart. When the link to a core router fails, the edge router has no backup neighbour. One edge router can tunnel to the other core router instead.

sections.title: Protection in Real Networks
sections.content:
The document reports the results of analysing a number of real world service provider topologies collected between the end of 2012 and early 2013. Fourteen topologies were studied, ranging from 55 nodes and 237 links to 1281 nodes and 2326 links. For each, the study measured the percentage of destinations protected against link failure, first using only LFA repairs and then using remote LFA.

With LFA alone, the protected share of destinations ranges from 78.5% in topology 1 to 99.6% in topology 11. Remote LFA provides close to 100% prefix protection against link failure in 11 of the 14 topologies studied and provides a significant improvement in two of the remaining three cases. Topology 1 goes from 78.5% to 99.7%, topology 4 from 83.1% to 99%, topology 6 from 86.4% to 100% and topology 9 from 82.2% to 99.5%. The guaranteed node protecting share changes much less, usually by a few percentage points, because remote LFA is aimed at link failures.

In the study, remote LFA was used only when necessary: when at least one destination was not repairable by a per-destination LFA, a single remote LFA tunnel was used for all such destinations, with the repair target computed from the extended P-space and the PQ node that has the lowest metric cost from the repairing node. The number of unidirectional targeted LDP sessions ranged from 7 to 1424 across the topologies, and the number of cases where neither LFA nor RLFA protection was possible because there was no PQ node ranged from 0 to 95. In an MPLS network, the tunnels to the PQ nodes are always present as a property of an LDP-based deployment.

The management of LFA and remote LFA is the subject of ongoing work within the IETF, and management considerations may lead to a preference for using a remote LFA over an available LFA. That preference is a matter for the network operator and not a matter of protocol correctness. When the network reconverges, micro-loops can form because of transient inconsistencies in the forwarding tables of different routers. If micro-loops are determined to be a significant issue in the deployment, a suitable loop-free convergence method should be implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: The document tested 14 real service provider networks. Plain fast reroute protected between 78.5% and 99.6% of destinations. With the tunnel, 11 of the 14 reached nearly 100% protection against link failure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5286 also apply. Targeted LDP sessions and MPLS tunnels are normal features of an MPLS network, and their use in this application raises no additional security concerns.

IP repair tunnel endpoints, where used, SHOULD be assigned from a set of addresses that are not reachable from outside the routing domain, which would prevent their use as an attack vector. Other than OAM traffic used to verify the correct operation of a repair tunnel, only traffic that is being protected as a result of a link failure is placed in a repair tunnel. The repair tunnel MUST NOT be advertised by the routing protocol as a link that may be used to carry normal user traffic or routing protocol traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel is only for traffic that a failure has displaced. The router must not offer it as a normal path, or other traffic could be sent down it. Tunnel addresses should not be reachable from outside the network.

viz.caption: THE SETS AND NODES THE RFC DEFINES

items.title: P-space
items.text: Routers the repairing router can reach without using the failed link.

items.title: Extended P-space
items.text: The union of the P-spaces of the repairing router's neighbours, with the one behind the failed link left out.

items.title: Q-space
items.text: Routers that can reach the far end of the failed link without using it.

items.title: PQ node
items.text: A router in both the extended P-space and the Q-space. It becomes the repair tunnel endpoint.
